3'-5' linkage joining nucleotides in a polynucleotide chain; forms backbone of nucleic acids
Watson-Crick model of DNA (1953); two anti-parallel polynucleotide chains coiled right-handed; bases inside, sugar-phosphate backbone outside
In double-stranded DNA, A=T and G=C (purine:pyrimidine = 1); basis for complementary base pairing
Complementary bases joined by H-bonds: A–T (2 H-bonds) and G–C (3 H-bonds); confers complementarity to strands
The two strands of DNA run in opposite directions: one 5'→3', the other 3'→5'
Francis Crick: genetic information flows DNA → RNA → Protein; reversed in retroviruses (RNA → DNA)
Positively charged basic protein (rich in lysine and arginine); forms octamer around which DNA wraps; packaging of DNA
Eight histone molecules forming a spool; 200 bp of DNA wraps around it to form nucleosome
Basic packaging unit of chromatin; 200 bp DNA wrapped around histone octamer; "beads-on-string" structure
Complex of DNA and proteins in nucleus; forms chromosomes during cell division; composed of repeating nucleosomes
Loosely packed chromatin; stains light; transcriptionally active
Densely packed chromatin; stains dark; transcriptionally inactive
Proteins required for higher-level chromatin packaging beyond nucleosome
Griffith (1928): heat-killed virulent S strain transforms non-virulent R strain of Streptococcus pneumoniae; first evidence for genetic material
Avery, MacLeod, McCarty (1933-44): DNA alone is the transforming principle; DNA is hereditary material
1952: used radioactive 32P (DNA) and 35S (protein) to prove DNA (not protein) is the genetic material in bacteriophages
Each replicated DNA contains one original + one new strand; proposed by Watson-Crick; proved by Meselson-Stahl (1958) using 15N labelling
1958: grew E. coli on 15N medium then switched to 14N; CsCl density gradient showed hybrid then light DNA, proving semiconservative replication
Main enzyme of replication; uses DNA template to polymerise deoxyribonucleotides; works only 5'→3'
Local opening of DNA helix where replication occurs; formed because entire DNA cannot unwind at once
Definite region in DNA where replication initiates; E. coli has one; vectors provide it for recombinant DNA work
Short DNA fragments synthesised discontinuously on the lagging strand (5'→3' template); later joined by DNA ligase
Enzyme that joins Okazaki fragments and seals nicks in DNA strand; essential for completing replication
Process of copying genetic information from template strand of DNA into RNA; complementarity-based; one strand copied
DNA strand with 3'→5' polarity; used as template during transcription; also called antisense strand
DNA strand with 5'→3' polarity; has same sequence as RNA (except T instead of U); not transcribed
Segment of DNA flanked by promoter (upstream) and terminator (downstream) plus structural gene; unit of transcription
DNA sequence upstream of structural gene; binding site for RNA polymerase; determines template and coding strands
DNA sequence downstream of structural gene; signals end of transcription; RNA polymerase and nascent RNA fall off
Enzyme that catalyses transcription; polymerises ribonucleotides; single type in bacteria (uses σ and ρ factors)
RNA carrying genetic information from DNA to ribosome; provides template for translation; from RNA pol II in eukaryotes
Adapter molecule; has anticodon loop and amino acid acceptor end; reads genetic code; brings amino acids to ribosome
Structural and catalytic component of ribosome; 23S rRNA acts as ribozyme catalysing peptide bond formation
mRNA coding for a single polypeptide; typical of eukaryotes
mRNA coding for more than one polypeptide; typical of bacteria/prokaryotes
Coding sequence in a eukaryotic gene; present in mature/processed mRNA; expressed sequence
Intervening sequence in eukaryotic gene; removed during RNA processing (splicing); not in mature mRNA
Removal of introns and joining of exons in pre-mRNA to produce functional mRNA; occurs in nucleus
Primary transcript in eukaryotes; contains exons and introns; undergoes capping, tailing, splicing to become mRNA
Addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate to 5'-end of hnRNA; part of mRNA processing in eukaryotes
Addition of 200–300 adenylate residues to 3'-end of hnRNA; template-independent; part of mRNA processing
Triplet set of codons specifying amino acids; 64 codons total (61 sense + 3 stop); degenerate and nearly universal
Set of three consecutive nucleotides in mRNA coding for one amino acid; 61 code for amino acids, 3 are stop codons
Triplet on tRNA complementary to mRNA codon; reads the genetic code; located on anticodon loop
Most amino acids coded by more than one codon; 20 amino acids encoded by 61 codons
AUG codes for methionine and acts as initiation codon; recognised by initiator tRNA
UAA, UAG, UGA; do not code for any amino acid; signal termination of translation; no corresponding tRNA
Same codon specifies same amino acid in most organisms from bacteria to humans; exceptions in mitochondria and some protozoans
Process of polymerisation of amino acids as directed by mRNA sequence; occurs at ribosome; produces polypeptide
Activation of amino acid with ATP and its attachment to cognate tRNA; energy for peptide bond formation
Covalent bond joining amino acids in a polypeptide; formed at ribosome (23S rRNA/ribozyme); requires energy
Cellular factory for protein synthesis; two subunits (large + small); contains rRNA and ~80 proteins
mRNA sequences at 5' and 3' ends flanking coding sequence; required for efficient translation
Cluster of prokaryotic genes under single promoter/operator regulation; all genes encode enzymes of same pathway
Jacob and Monod model operon in E. coli; i gene (repressor) + promoter/operator + z (β-gal) + y (permease) + a (transacetylase); regulated by lactose
Protein encoded by regulatory gene; binds operator and blocks RNA polymerase; inactivated by inducer in negative regulation
Molecule that inactivates repressor, allowing transcription of operon; e.g., lactose/allolactose for lac operon
DNA sequence adjacent to promoter; binding site for repressor; controls access of RNA polymerase to structural genes
Mega project (1990–2003); sequenced all ~3×10⁹ bp of human genome; identified ~20,000–25,000 genes; led to bioinformatics
Use of computational tools for storage, retrieval and analysis of biological sequence data; grew with HGP
Single base pair differences among individuals; ~1.4 million locations in humans; used for disease mapping and genetic tracing
Vector used in HGP to clone large DNA fragments in bacteria; provides origin of replication
Vector used in HGP to clone very large DNA fragments in yeast; handles larger inserts than BAC
Approach in HGP sequencing only expressed (RNA) sequences; identifies genes that are transcribed
Technique to compare DNA sequences of individuals using polymorphic VNTR regions; developed by Alec Jeffreys; forensic, paternity, biodiversity applications
Class of satellite DNA (mini-satellite); copy number varies per chromosome; basis of DNA fingerprinting probe
Repetitive DNA separating from bulk genomic DNA as distinct peak in density gradient; includes microsatellites and mini-satellites
Inheritable variation in DNA sequence present at frequency >0.01 in population; basis of DNA fingerprinting and genetic mapping
Technique: DNA fragments separated by electrophoresis → transferred to membrane → hybridised with labelled probe → autoradiography; used in DNA fingerprinting
RNA was the first genetic material and catalyst; life processes evolved around RNA; DNA derived from RNA by chemical modification
Origin of universe; singular huge explosion ~13.8 billion years ago; hydrogen and helium formed; galaxies condensed under gravitation
Oparin-Haldane hypothesis: formation of organic molecules (amino acids, sugars, bases) from inorganic compounds before life arose; first step toward life
S.L. Miller (1953): electric discharge through CH₄, H₂, NH₃, water vapour at 800°C produced amino acids, simulating early Earth conditions
Hypothesis that life (spores) came to Earth from outer space; proposed by early Greek thinkers; favoured by some astronomers
Discredited theory that life arises from non-living matter; disproved by Louis Pasteur's experiments with sterilised flasks
Principle that life arises only from pre-existing life; established by Pasteur; accepted view of life's continuity
Remains or impressions of hard parts of life-forms found in sedimentary rock layers; primary evidence for evolution
Evidence for evolution from study of fossils in different sedimentary layers; shows different life forms at different geological time periods
Organs with similar anatomical structure but different functions; derived from same ancestral origin; indicate divergent evolution and common ancestry; e.g., forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah, human
Organs with similar functions but different anatomical structure; result of convergent evolution; e.g., wings of butterfly and bird, eyes of octopus and mammal
Evolution of different forms from a common ancestor; leads to homologous structures; e.g., Darwin's finches, Australian marsupials
Independent evolution of similar features in unrelated organisms in similar environments; leads to analogous structures
Evolution of different species from a single ancestral form radiating into different habitats; e.g., Darwin's finches of Galapagos, Australian marsupials
14 species of finches in Galapagos Islands; classic example of adaptive radiation; beak shape adapted to food type
Darwin's mechanism of evolution; heritable variations conferring better survival are selected; selected individuals reproduce more and leave greater progeny
Reproductive fitness; ability of organism to survive and reproduce in its environment; ultimately measured by number of progeny
Key concept of Darwinian theory; new species arise from pre-existing ones; all life shares common ancestors
Lamarck's theory: evolution driven by use and disuse of organs; acquired characters inherited; e.g., giraffe's neck; now discredited
Mutations (large sudden changes) cause evolution (saltation); contrasts with Darwin's gradual small variations; based on work on evening primrose
Single-step large mutation causing speciation; proposed by Hugo de Vries; opposite of Darwin's gradual change
Allele frequencies in a population remain stable across generations (genetic equilibrium) unless disturbed; p² + 2pq + q² = 1
Total of all genes and their alleles in a population; remains constant under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
State where allele frequencies in a population remain constant generation to generation; maintained under Hardy-Weinberg conditions
Movement of alleles between populations through migration; changes allele frequencies in both source and recipient populations
Random change in allele frequency due to chance events; more pronounced in small populations; can lead to speciation
Genetic drift when small group establishes new population; new population may have different allele frequencies from original
Formation of new species from existing ones; results from accumulated genetic changes separating populations reproductively
Natural selection example: dark moths survived post-industrialisation when tree trunks darkened; white moths survived pre-industrialisation; camouflage drives selection
Natural selection favouring mean phenotype; reduces variation; most individuals cluster around mean value
Natural selection favouring one extreme phenotype; shifts population mean in one direction; e.g., antibiotic resistance
Natural selection favouring both extremes of phenotypic range; increases variation; may lead to two distinct forms
Early hominid; ~2 mya; lived in East African grasslands; walked upright; hunted with stone weapons; ate fruit
First human-like hominid; ~2 mya; brain 650–800 cc; used stone tools; probably did not eat meat
~1.5 mya; fossil found in Java (1891); brain ~900 cc; ate meat
~1,00,000–40,000 years ago; near east and central Asia; brain ~1400 cc; used hides; buried dead
Modern humans; arose in Africa ~75,000–10,000 years ago during ice age; cave art ~18,000 years ago; agriculture ~10,000 years ago
Primate ~15 mya; more ape-like; walked like gorillas and chimpanzees
Primate ~15 mya; more man-like than Dryopithecus
Lobe-finned fish thought to be extinct; live specimen found in South Africa (1938); represents transition to land vertebrates
Fish (~350 mya) → amphibians → reptiles → mammals → primates; geological periods correlate with biological changes
State of complete physical, mental and social well-being; not merely absence of disease
Disease-causing organism (bacteria, virus, fungus, protozoan, helminth) that multiplies in host and causes harm
Caused by Salmonella typhi; spreads through contaminated food/water; symptoms: high fever (39–40°C), headache, stomach pain; confirmed by Widal test
Diagnostic blood test for typhoid fever; detects antibodies against Salmonella typhi antigens
Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae; alveoli fill with fluid; symptoms: fever, chills, cough; spreads by aerosols
Caused by rhinoviruses; affects nose and respiratory passage; nasal congestion, sore throat, cough; lasts 3–7 days; spreads by droplets
Caused by Plasmodium (protozoan); transmitted by female Anopheles mosquito; P. falciparum causes most fatal malignant malaria
Protozoan parasite causing malaria; species: P. vivax, P. malariae, P. falciparum; two hosts: human and female Anopheles mosquito
Infectious form of Plasmodium; inoculated into human by mosquito bite; initially multiplies in liver cells
Toxic substance released when Plasmodium ruptures RBCs; causes chill and recurring high fever in malaria
Caused by Entamoeba histolytica in large intestine; symptoms: constipation, abdominal pain, bloody mucous stools; transmitted via contaminated food/water
Caused by Ascaris (roundworm); intestinal parasite; spreads through contaminated water/food; internal bleeding, muscular pain, anaemia
Caused by Wuchereria bancrofti or W. malayi; filarial worms in lymph vessels; transmitted by female mosquito vectors; gross deformity of affected organ
Fungal infection by Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton; dry scaly lesions on skin, nails, scalp; intense itching; thrives in moist warm conditions
Overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms; conferred by immune system; innate and acquired types
Non-specific, present at birth; four types of barriers: physical (skin, mucus), physiological (acid, saliva, tears), cellular (phagocytes, NK cells), cytokine (interferons)
Pathogen-specific; characterised by memory; primary (low intensity) and secondary/anamnestic (high intensity) responses; mediated by B and T lymphocytes
Produces antibodies (proteins) in response to pathogens; humoral immune response; produces memory cells
Cell-mediated immunity; helper T-cells assist B-cells; cytotoxic T-cells kill infected cells; memory T-cells
Protein (H₂L₂) produced by B-cells; specific to antigen; types: IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG; neutralises pathogens
Antibody-mediated immunity; B-lymphocytes produce antibodies that circulate in blood and fight antigens
T-lymphocyte-mediated immune response; responsible for graft rejection; kills infected/abnormal cells directly
Immunity produced when host is exposed to antigens (vaccination or natural infection); slow to develop; long-lasting memory
Ready-made antibodies given to host; immediate protection; no memory; e.g., colostrum (IgA), antitoxin, anti-venom
Yellowish fluid secreted by mother in first days of lactation; rich in IgA antibodies; provides passive immunity to newborn
Introduction of weakened/killed pathogen or its antigens to stimulate immune memory; prevents disease on future exposure
Antigen causing exaggerated immune response (allergy); e.g., pollen, dust mites, animal dander; triggers IgE production
Exaggerated immune response to allergens; symptoms: sneezing, watery eyes, difficulty breathing; mediated by histamine and serotonin from mast cells
Body attacks its own cells due to failure of self-non-self recognition; e.g., rheumatoid arthritis
Organs of immune system; primary (bone marrow, thymus) and secondary (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, MALT, Peyer's patches)
Primary lymphoid organ near heart; site of T-lymphocyte maturation; large at birth, decreases with age
Lymphoid tissue in lining of respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts; ~50% of lymphoid tissue in human body
Caused by HIV (retrovirus); progressive depletion of helper T-cells; immune deficiency; fatal; first reported 1981
Retrovirus causing AIDS; RNA genome; uses reverse transcriptase; infects macrophages and helper T-lymphocytes; transmitted through blood, sexual contact, placenta, needles
Enzyme used by retroviruses (HIV) to synthesise viral DNA from RNA genome; target of anti-retroviral drugs
Diagnostic test for AIDS/HIV; detects antibodies against HIV in patient's blood
Uncontrolled cell division due to loss of contact inhibition; forms tumors; major cause of death worldwide
Non-cancerous mass; confined to original location; does not spread; causes little damage
Cancerous mass; rapidly dividing neoplastic cells; invades surrounding tissues; can metastasise
Spread of cancer cells from primary tumor through blood to distant sites forming secondary tumors; most feared property of malignant tumors
Property of normal cells to stop dividing when they come into contact with other cells; lost in cancer cells
Agent inducing cancer: physical (X-rays, UV), chemical (tobacco smoke), biological (oncogenic viruses)
Gene causing cancer; viral oncogenes (v-onc) and cellular oncogenes/proto-oncogenes (c-onc) that activate abnormally
Drugs binding opioid receptors in CNS; heroin (diacetylmorphine) derived from Papaver somniferum; depressant; highly addictive
Group of chemicals from Cannabis sativa interacting with cannabinoid receptors in brain; includes marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja; affect cardiovascular system
From Erythroxylum coca; stimulant acting on CNS; interferes with dopamine transport; produces euphoria; hallucinations at excess dose
Alkaloid in tobacco; stimulates adrenal gland to release adrenaline/noradrenaline; raises blood pressure and heart rate; addictive
Performance-enhancing drugs abused by athletes; cause serious side-effects including masculinisation in females, reduced sperm production in males
Psychological and physical attachment to drugs/alcohol; driven by perceived benefits; tolerance increases requiring higher doses
Unpleasant symptoms (anxiety, nausea, sweating) when regular drug/alcohol use is abruptly stopped; indicates dependence
Bacteria (Lactobacillus and others) growing in milk; produce acids coagulating milk proteins converting milk to curd; also increase vitamin B12
Anaerobic metabolic process by microbes producing organic compounds and gases; used in curd, bread, beverages, cheese production
Baker's/brewer's yeast; used for bread fermentation (produces CO2) and ethanol production in alcoholic beverages
Fermented milk product; texture, flavour and taste determined by specific microbes; e.g., Propionibacterium sharmanii for Swiss cheese holes; fungi for Roquefort
Large vessel for growing microbes on industrial scale; used in antibiotic, enzyme, biogas and beverage production
Chemical produced by microbe killing or retarding growth of other (disease-causing) microbes; e.g., penicillin
First antibiotic discovered (Fleming, 1928) from mould Penicillium notatum; effective against Staphylococci; Nobel Prize 1945 (Fleming, Chain, Florey)
Enzyme produced by Streptococcus; modified by genetic engineering; used as clot buster in myocardial infarction patients
Immunosuppressive drug produced by fungus Trichoderma polysporum; used in organ-transplant patients to prevent rejection
Blood-cholesterol-lowering agents produced by yeast Monascus purpureus; competitively inhibit enzyme for cholesterol synthesis
Municipal waste water containing human excreta, organic matter and pathogens; treated in sewage treatment plants before disposal
Amount of oxygen consumed to oxidise all organic matter in 1 litre of water by bacteria; measure of organic pollution level
Physical removal of floating debris (filtration) and grit/solids (sedimentation) from sewage; produces primary sludge and effluent
Biological treatment of primary effluent; aerobic microbes in aeration tanks consume organic matter; reduces BOD; produces activated sludge
Sediment of bacterial flocs after secondary treatment; small portion recycled as inoculum; rest goes to anaerobic sludge digesters
Masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments forming mesh-like structures in aeration tanks during sewage treatment
Large tank where activated sludge is digested by anaerobic bacteria; produces biogas (methane, H2S, CO2)
Mixture of gases (mainly methane) produced by microbial activity on organic matter; used as fuel for cooking and lighting; gobar gas in rural areas
Methanogen bacterium; grows anaerobically on cellulosic material; produces methane; present in anaerobic sludge and cattle rumen
Methane-producing bacteria growing anaerobically; found in sewage sludge and rumen of cattle; basis of biogas production
Use of biological methods (natural predators, microbes) to control plant pests and diseases; reduces dependence on toxic chemicals
Bacterium used as biocontrol agent against butterfly caterpillars/insect larvae; spores sprayed on plants; toxin released in larval gut kills them; Bt-toxin gene introduced into Bt-cotton
Virus attacking insects and arthropods; used as biocontrol agent; genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus; species-specific, no effect on non-target organisms
Organism enriching soil nutrient quality; bacteria (Rhizobium, Azospirillum, Azotobacter), fungi (mycorrhiza), cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc)
Symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules of leguminous plants; converts atmospheric N2 into organic forms
Symbiotic association of fungi (e.g., Glomus) with plant roots; fungus absorbs phosphorus; plant gains nutrients, drought tolerance, pathogen resistance
Autotrophic nitrogen-fixing microbes; e.g., Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria; important biofertiliser in paddy fields; add organic matter to soil
Holistic approach combining biocontrol and other methods to manage pests; conserves beneficial insects while controlling harmful ones
Fungus used for commercial production of citric acid
Bacterium used for commercial production of acetic acid
Use of live organisms or enzymes to produce products and processes useful to humans; includes genetic engineering, in vitro fertilisation, gene therapy
Techniques to alter chemistry of genetic material (DNA/RNA), introduce into host organisms, and change phenotype; core tool of modern biotechnology
Process of creating and using recombinant DNA; uses restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors, host organisms; first demonstrated by Cohen and Boyer (1972)
Artificially created DNA combining DNA from different sources/organisms; created by restriction enzyme cutting and ligation
Molecular scissors; enzyme that cuts DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences; makes sticky ends; named by genus, species, strain, order (e.g., EcoRI)
Specific palindromic DNA sequence (typically 6 bp) recognised and cut by restriction endonuclease; e.g., 5'-GAATTC-3' for EcoRI
DNA sequence reading the same on both strands in 5'→3' direction; recognition site for restriction enzymes
Single-stranded overhanging sequences produced after restriction enzyme cut; form H-bonds with complementary sticky ends; facilitate ligation
Nuclease enzyme that removes nucleotides from ends of DNA strand
Technique separating DNA fragments by size in agarose gel under electric field; DNA (negatively charged) moves toward anode; smaller fragments move farther
Natural polymer from seaweed used as matrix in gel electrophoresis to separate DNA fragments by size
Fluorescent stain for DNA in gel electrophoresis; gives bright orange bands under UV light
Extraction of DNA band from agarose gel piece after electrophoresis; purified fragment used in cloning
DNA molecule (plasmid, phage) used to carry foreign DNA into host cell; must have ori, selectable marker, cloning site; multiplies in host
Autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA in bacteria; used as cloning vector; e.g., pBR322
Specific DNA sequence where replication starts; every cloning vector must have ori for alien DNA to replicate in host; controls copy number
Gene in cloning vector (e.g., antibiotic resistance) allowing selection of transformed cells from non-transformants
Common E. coli cloning vector; has ampicillin and tetracycline resistance genes, multiple restriction sites, and ori
Disruption of selectable marker gene by insertion of foreign DNA; recombinant clones identified because marker gene becomes non-functional (e.g., no blue colour)
Pathogen of dicot plants; delivers T-DNA causing tumors; Ti plasmid disarmed and used as cloning vector to transfer genes into plants
Tumor-inducing plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens; modified as vector to deliver desired genes into plant cells
Procedure introducing foreign DNA (recombinant plasmid) into a competent host bacterium
Bacterial cell made capable of taking up foreign DNA; achieved by treatment with divalent cations (Ca2+) followed by heat shock (42°C)
Direct injection of recombinant DNA into nucleus of animal cell using a fine needle
Method of introducing DNA into plant cells; cells bombarded with high-velocity DNA-coated gold or tungsten micro-particles
In vitro DNA amplification using primers and thermostable DNA polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus); three steps per cycle: denaturation, annealing, extension; amplifies to ~billion copies
Short synthetic oligonucleotide complementary to target DNA region; needed for PCR; directs DNA polymerase where to start
Thermophilic bacterium; source of thermostable Taq DNA polymerase used in PCR; remains active at high denaturation temperatures
Protein produced when a cloned gene is expressed in a heterologous (different) host organism
Large vessel (100–1000 litres) for growing cells to produce biotechnological products; provides optimal conditions: temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrients; stirred-tank most common
Post-biosynthesis steps: separation, purification, formulation and quality control of biotechnological product before marketing
Making multiple identical copies of a gene by inserting it into vector, introducing into host, and allowing it to replicate
Organism whose genes have been altered by manipulation using techniques like recombinant DNA technology; includes GM plants, bacteria, fungi, animals
In vitro technique growing plant cells/explants in sterile nutrient media; based on totipotency; used for micropropagation, virus-free plants
Any part of a plant taken out and grown in culture; source tissue for tissue culture; can regenerate whole plant
Capacity of any plant cell/explant to grow into a complete organism; basis of tissue culture and micropropagation
Production of thousands of genetically identical plants (somaclones) by tissue culture; used commercially for tomato, banana, apple
Plant produced by micropropagation; genetically identical to parent plant
Fusion of protoplasts from two different plant varieties to produce hybrid plants; e.g., pomato (tomato + potato protoplast fusion)
Transgenic cotton with Bacillus thuringiensis cry genes (cryIAc, cryIIAb); produces insecticidal protein crystal; resistant to cotton bollworm
Insecticidal protein produced by B. thuringiensis; inactive protoxin activated by alkaline pH of insect gut; binds to midgut epithelial cells causing pores and cell lysis
Genes encoding Bt toxin in Bacillus thuringiensis; e.g., cryIAc (cotton bollworm), cryIAb (corn borer), cryIIAb; used in GM crops
Cellular defence mechanism in eukaryotes; dsRNA silences specific mRNA by preventing translation; used to create nematode-resistant tobacco plants
GM rice enriched with vitamin A (beta-carotene); developed to address vitamin A deficiency; example of nutritionally enhanced GM crop
Human insulin produced in E. coli using rDNA technology; Eli Lilly (1983); chains A and B produced separately, combined by disulfide bonds; replaces animal-derived insulin
Extra stretch in proinsulin removed during maturation to form active insulin; not present in mature insulin
Collection of methods to correct gene defects by inserting functional genes into patient's cells; first used in 1990 for ADA deficiency
Adenosine deaminase deficiency; hereditary immune disorder; first treated by gene therapy (1990) using retroviral vector to introduce functional ADA cDNA into lymphocytes
Animal with manipulated DNA possessing and expressing a foreign gene; e.g., mice, Rosie (transgenic cow); used for disease models, biological products, vaccine testing
Early detection of disease using rDNA technology, PCR and ELISA; detects pathogens at very low concentration before symptoms appear
Single-stranded DNA/RNA tagged with radioactive molecule; hybridises to complementary sequence; used to detect mutations by autoradiography
Indian government body making decisions on validity of GM research and safety of introducing GM organisms for public services
Use of bio-resources by multinational companies without proper authorisation from countries/people and without compensatory payment
First transgenic cow (1997) producing human protein-enriched milk with alpha-lactalbumin (2.4 g/litre); more nutritionally balanced for human babies
Study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical (abiotic) environment; four levels: organisms, populations, communities, biomes
Group of individuals of the same species sharing resources in a defined geographical area; has attributes like birth rate, death rate, sex ratio, age distribution
Size of a population in a habitat; measured as number, biomass or per cent cover; fundamental parameter in ecology
Graphical representation of age distribution of males and females in a population; shape indicates if population is growing, stable or declining
Number of births added to a population during a given period; contributes to increase in population density
Number of deaths in a population during a given period; contributes to decrease in population density
Number of individuals moving into a population from elsewhere; increases population density
Number of individuals leaving a population; decreases population density
Parameter r = b - d (birth rate minus death rate); measures inherent growth potential of population; key in exponential growth equation dN/dt = rN
Unlimited population growth when resources are unrestricted; J-shaped curve; equation: dN/dt = rN; Nt = N0e^rt
Population growth with limited resources; S-shaped (sigmoid) curve; Verhulst-Pearl equation: dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K; more realistic model
Maximum population size a habitat can support with available resources; population stabilises at K in logistic growth
Interaction between populations of two different species; can be mutualism (+/+), competition (-/-), predation (+/-), parasitism (+/-), commensalism (+/0), amensalism (-/0)
Interaction where predator kills and eats prey; transfers energy to higher trophic levels; keeps prey populations in check
Both species suffer when competing for limiting resources; competitive exclusion principle: superior competitor eliminates inferior one (Gause)
Gause's principle: two closely related species competing for same resources cannot coexist indefinitely; competitively inferior species will be eliminated
Mechanism enabling co-existing species to avoid competition by using resources differently (different times, locations, strategies)
One species (parasite) benefits; host is harmed; ectoparasites on surface, endoparasites inside host; often involves intermediate hosts/vectors
Parasitic bird lays eggs in host bird's nest; host incubates them; parasite eggs mimic host eggs; e.g., cuckoo and crow
One species benefits; other neither benefited nor harmed; e.g., cattle egret and grazing cattle, orchid on mango tree, barnacles on whale
One species is harmed; other is unaffected; e.g., Penicillium secreting penicillin harming bacteria
Both species benefit from interaction; e.g., lichens (fungus + algae/cyanobacteria), mycorrhiza (fungus + plant roots), fig tree + wasp
Parasite living on external surface of host; e.g., lice on humans, ticks on dogs, Cuscuta on hedge plants
Parasite living inside host body (liver, kidney, RBCs etc.); simplified morphology; complex life cycle; e.g., Plasmodium, tapeworm
Species whose removal causes dramatic loss of biodiversity through competitive exclusion; e.g., starfish Pisaster in rocky intertidal communities
Functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with surrounding physical environment; e.g., pond, forest, grassland
Vertical distribution of different species at different levels in an ecosystem; e.g., trees (top), shrubs (middle), herbs/grasses (bottom) in forest
Amount of biomass/organic matter produced per unit area per time by plants during photosynthesis; expressed as g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹
Total rate of organic matter produced during photosynthesis in an ecosystem; includes biomass used in plant respiration
GPP minus respiration losses (R); biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs; NPP = GPP - R
Rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers; energy assimilated by heterotrophs from consumed food
Dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead animal matter including fecal material; raw material for decomposition
Breakdown of complex organic detritus into inorganic substances (CO2, water, nutrients) by decomposers; steps: fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation
Organism (e.g., earthworm) breaking down detritus into smaller particles by fragmentation; starts decomposition process
Breakdown of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores; first step of decomposition
Water-soluble inorganic nutrients moving down into soil horizon and precipitating as unavailable salts; step in decomposition
Accumulation of dark amorphous humus from decomposed organic matter; highly resistant to microbial action; slow decomposition rate
Dark coloured amorphous substance formed during decomposition; colloidal; reservoir of nutrients; slowly mineralised by microbes
Release of inorganic nutrients from humus by microbial degradation; final step making nutrients available for reuse by plants
Portion of solar radiation (less than 50%) usable for photosynthesis; plants capture only 2–10% of PAR
Linear sequence of organisms where each feeds on the one below it; energy transfer from producers to consumers; restricted by 10% law
Food chain beginning with living plant matter; producers → herbivores → carnivores; major energy conduit in aquatic ecosystems
Food chain beginning with dead organic matter; decomposers (fungi, bacteria) break down detritus; dominant in terrestrial ecosystems
Natural interconnection of multiple food chains; more realistic representation of energy flow; omnivores link different chains
Position of organism in food chain based on feeding relationship; producers = first, herbivores = second, carnivores = third trophic level
Only 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next trophic level; limits number of trophic levels in a food chain
Mass of living organisms (biomass) or number of individuals at a particular trophic level at a given time; measured as fresh or dry weight
Graphical representation of relationship between organisms at different trophic levels; types: pyramid of number, biomass, energy
Always upright; never inverted; energy at lower trophic level always greater than higher; shows progressive energy loss at each step
Storage and movement of nutrient elements through various ecosystem components; nutrients repeatedly reused; gaseous type (carbon, nitrogen) and sedimentary type (phosphorus)
Decomposer organism (fungi, bacteria) obtaining energy by degrading dead organic matter; secretes digestive enzymes externally
Term popularised by Edward Wilson; sum total of diversity at all levels of biological organisation — genetic, species, and ecological
